items.title: 亲眼目睹之后，我确信《魔兽世界：永远》的 RP 服务器不需要如此独立，而且作为 MMO 角色扮演领域的资深人士，我这么说
items.summary: I'm kinda just playing chiller PvE, here.

content.v: I've been stuck into World of Warcraft: Forever —at the time of writing, I'm around 15 hours /played (and will likely be 20+ hours by the time you're reading this) on my warrior. I chose the roleplay ruleset because, well, I'm a roleplayer. I've been writing and being cringe in videogames for over 15 years .

RP in WoW is, actually, what got me into writing in the first place. My clear and obvious mastery over the written word was hard-won by being a terribly annoying edgelord death knight, for which I apologise.

I was curious about the implementation of the roleplay ruleset back when it was properly announced—back then, I thought it was great that we're being given our own place, but being completely split off from "normal" ruleset (which I'll be calling PvE for simplicity) didn't seem necessary to me.

Having played in the roleplay ruleset for a little while, my opinion has only been vindicated. Splitting PvE and PvP rulesets does make sense. For instance, a resource node might be easier to gather on PvE, throwing the economic balance of the PvP server out of the window. But beyond technical limitations, a complete, strict divide between RP and PvE just has me scratching my head.

There are things I like about having our own little nook of the Forever servers to putz about on. For starters, the vibes are a lot chiller. I don't want to cast generalisations about players, but I do think roleplayers are just smarter, sexier, have bigger muscles, and will solve climate change.

In seriousness, I do think thinking about your character's place in the world and having a bent towards immersion does make you a chiller person in general. I've experienced vanishingly little toxicity or hostility. The absolute worst instance was a tank getting a little passive-aggressive about mining nodes in my Deadmines run. That's it.

But what I foresaw is bearing out: Nobody is really roleplaying in instanced or group content, and that's because we legitimately never have done so. Most RP takes place either spontaneously out in the open world, or in dedicated hot spots. Even in the most diehard MMO communities, people aren't talking in ye olde English while pushing Vancleef's face in.
There are some people who are always in-character, sure, but that portion of the playerbase is incredibly rare. We're talking a sliver of an already-small population of a videogame, here.
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/ahEGtzYgdtscBynSWUZPNn-1920-80.png

As for the strict rules on naming conventions—yeah, I'm seeing a lot more lore-accurate names, but I'm also seeing plenty of joke ones. And if I'm being perfectly honest, these gag names really haven't ever bothered me; people being disruptive or annoying when I'm roleplaying are a massive pain, but if Tsundere Cowbell the paladin wants to watch me write, my immersion isn't shattered.

Overall, I think keeping us on our own server architecture for the most part is the smarter plan, especially given layering would dilute roleplayers so much that RP would be hard to find. However, I don't think there's any real reason to disallow us from jumping to the Normal ruleset servers when we group up with someone from there—or giving us an option to travel between them of our own accord.

Just as we tend to swap between in-character for roleplay and out-of-character for, y'know, playing the videogame—I think most of us would be happy to have the choice as to whether we want to futz about on the roleplay layer or go hang out with our non-theatre kid friends on the PvE ruleset.

Especially given, as time goes on, population might become an issue. Believe it or not, roleplayers still do like to raid and gear up, and if they should be able to migrate on characters they've invested literal dozens of hours into, rather than having to start all over again.

items.title: 《质量效应》演员通过视频庆祝 N7 日，请求粉丝帮助拯救该系列
items.summary: Without BioWare, N7 Day is quieter this year, but that didn't stop the Normandy cast and crew from teaming up

content.v: https://assets-prd.ignimgs.com/2026/08/17/me1-blogroll-1786972844387.jpg
Without BioWare, N7 Day is quieter this year, but that didn't stop the Normandy cast and crew from teaming up for a video message asking fans to help save Mass Effect.

EA shuttered BioWare , canceled Mass Effect 5 , and put the gaming side of the franchise on an indefinite hold just weeks before the series' annual November 7 holiday, leaving players just as hurt as they were confused. There's not really any official festivities to enjoy this year, but the developers and actors behind the stories and characters fans love still made sure to get together for a special video message.

Organized by the unofficial group known as We are Mass Effect, the two-minute video message features appearances from composer Sam Hulick, Jennifer Hale (Commander Shepard/FemShep), Ash Sroka (Tali'Zorah), Keythe Farley (Thane), Kimberly Brooks (Ashley), Mark Meer (Commander Shepard/MaleShep), Steve Blum (Urdnot Grunt), Brandon Keener (Garrus), and many more. One by one, they each call to "Save Mass Effect" in the wake of BioWare's closure, marking what is only the latest shot to garner attention and, hopefully, give the franchise a shot in the arm.

Today is a very special day for Mass Effect fans. We've worked incredibly hard to bring together most of the original Mass Effect trilogy's voice cast to share a very important message with you. We need to #SaveMassEffect. https://t.co/FOp0qp4wBI

"It started feeling like Shepard recruiting the squad in Mass Effect 2!" We are Mass Effect's Mer told IGN when describing the process to make the video. "We were bringing people on board one by one, and Mark was a huge help in making that happen! It almost felt like we were gathering War Assets. And the most surprising thing is that with every video we received, the actors would thank us.

"We'd get messages saying, 'Thank you for doing this,' or 'Thank you for your work.' We were the ones who felt incredibly grateful to them for taking the time to participate, but they kept turning around and thanking us. That really touched me. Everyone involved, from the people who made these games to the people who brought their characters to life, cares deeply about this universe."

We are Mass Effect and other Mass Effect fans have been busy the last few weeks. After footage and details for the canceled Mass Effect: Universe appeared online just days after EA brought the franchise to a halt, a petition has launched and gained more than 310,000 signatures . A Canadian politician also started a government petition to save BioWare just last week.

As some have called to boycott EA , others have taken their fight straight to the publisher's front door . We are Mass Effect has been a big part of that initiative, with its first and most notable move arriving when it launched a #SaveMassEffect billboard in Times Square . Yesterday, the group drove a mobile billboard around EA headquarters in Redwood City, California . More billboards are live today, including one posted up around the former BioWare offices in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, with another set to appear around The Game Awards next month. Former project director and executive producer Michael Gamble also sent a message to fans for N7 Day.

🚨 WE ARE IN EDMONTON Today, our mobile billboard is right outside BioWare's former offices. For 30 years, BioWare gave us unforgettable stories and characters. Today, we're standing up for the people who brought them to life. #SaveMassEffect https://t.co/fXa4bemyfE

🚨 WE'RE KICKING OFF N7 DAY WITH ANOTHER BILLBOARD This time, #SaveMassEffect has made its way to Cardiff, Wales, thanks to the incredible @psykit. Another amazing initiative from our community, showing that we're not giving up on Mass Effect and BioWare's legacy. https://t.co/4avNpk18jd

🚨 WE ARE TAKING OVER TEXAS A member of our community, AngryBaby, has put up #SaveMassEffect billboards in the Frisco and Dallas areas of North Texas. It's incredible to see fans taking the initiative and spreading the movement on their own. HOLD THE LINE 🫡 https://t.co/AoJBppCzbV
You all are truly amazing. The love and passion for this…universe…is incredible. Even in worst days, we could always count on you. To all the stories left untold. Happy N7 Day.

"We're still holding on to that hope and fighting for the future of Mass Effect, BioWare, and the people who have dedicated so much of themselves to bringing this universe to life," Mer added. "N7 Day is a reminder of what these games mean to all of us, but also of the people behind them. The impact they've had on this community will never been forgotten, and we will continue celebrating it for as long as we can."

Meanwhile, as the Mass Effect cast and fans on the ground do their best to celebrate N7 Day, other developers have chimed in to share their love for the series on its saddest holiday so far. Owlcat Games, the team behind the upcoming Mass Effect-inspired RPG The Expanse: Osiris Reborn, shared a video celebrating what BioWare and its work over the decades means to them.

"Everybody in Owlcat dreamt about playing Mass Effect 5," studio creative director Alexander Mishulin said. "It's very, very selfish, but we wanted to experience the next chapter in those adventures. Our hearts and minds are with [BioWare], and we really hope they find themselves a new home, different studios that will allow them to make even more worlds, even more experiences, more adventures that we will be amazed at. That will be new beacons for new generations of game developers.
This #N7Day is a sad one for all Mass Effect fans. So we want to reminisce about what Mass Effect and many other BioWare games meant to us and how they inspired us. https://t.co/HKG5XkLA28
"It will be not Mass Effect, but it will be something else, and something beautiful."

BioWare's final years were captured on video and will soon be shared in a new documentary . For more, you can check out IGN's interview with one modder who has rebuilt Mass Effect 3's multiplayer . You can also read about how AI is impacting the modding scene .

items.title: “我觉得改装已经快要死了”——质量效应 3 多人游戏改装者谈 AI 对场景的影响
items.summary: Over the past few months, there's been a sort of explosion of AI in the modding scene. Whether it's mashup mod

content.v: https://assets-prd.ignimgs.com/2026/10/29/me3-1793234529955.jpg

Over the past few months, there's been an explosion of AI in the modding scene. Whether it's mashup mods on Twitter or full decompilation done by Claude , AI is everywhere in the mod community, and it could be killing the hobby.

I got a chance to sit down with ME3Tweaks' Mgamerz to talk about his new Mass Effect Legendary Edition ME3 Multiplayer mod, where I asked him about how AI has affected the modding community. While he admits that Claude is very effective at modding games, it's causing an avalanche of low-effort content that's hard to sift through. And, while there has always been a range of quality for mods, the inherent difficulty of getting into a game's files and changing things was a natural filter that's slowly eroding.

Mgamerz told me, "The difficulty of making mods and getting into it filtered out a lot of low-quality stuff. You see this on stuff like the Switch eShop, I've heard. It's full of slop, because there's no quality control and you can just ship whatever, and then users have to dredge through all sorts of stuff like that."

Although typing in a prompt to mod your own copy of a game is one thing, the problems start to appear once you start distributing it on platforms like Nexus Mods, where you have to be mindful about how your mod will interact with other add-ons, otherwise you're likely to just break peoples' games.

Mgamerz laid out that process, telling me, "In the modding community, you have an ecosystem. For example, I have my mod manager, you deploy mods through the mod manager, it runs a bunch of checks on the mods to make sure you're not going to ship something that's just going to break someone's game immediately."

These AI mods can do more than just break other people's mods too — they can also make your game much harder to run if they aren't optimized properly. For example, Mgamerz says, "There's certain knowledge, like you don't put stuff in startup files because it wastes tons of memory. If you stuff everything in there, you boot the game, oh, now the game takes an extra gigabyte of memory for your single mod to work, because you didn't want to do it the proper way."

It's hard to argue with the fact that these AI tools are introducing a whole new generation of gamers to modding, but it's doing so without making them go through the effort of figuring out how to make things effectively. We've already seen major modding communities pull their sites down because of this outbreak of AI modding tools that can take months of someone's hard work and spin it around into a 'working' mod after a couple of Claude prompts. And that might end up becoming the default for people who learn how to code exclusively through AI tools.

When I asked Mgamerz what the pathway for people who want to get into modding these days is, his answer was grim. He told me, "Getting into [modding]? I feel like modding is kind of dying. If you come in and you're like, 'I want to just do this, no AI. I just want to cut my teeth, find the boundaries, break over them, have a difficult, challenging task,' you pretty much have to work in secret now."

"Because if you essentially have an idea and someone else is like, 'Wow, that's a cool idea.' And you're like, 'Well, it's going to take me six months.' And they're like, 'I don't want to wait six months.' They can spend 20 bucks and pump this thing out in a day or two, and it'll probably work, but the user will have no understanding of how."

Mgamerz understands, though, that the prevalence of these AI tools is getting a lot of people interested in modding their favorite games, and that's not a bad thing. He told me, "If you don't release the stuff that you make, I don't see any problem. You made something cool for yourself."

Instead, the problem is that, if you install it without considering how it'll interact with other software, it can really bungle other peoples' projects. "Once you hand this product over to somebody else, share it with the world, suddenly it can become everybody's problem. And from my experience, everyone that vibe codes stuff, two weeks later, they're gone. They're not supporting it. So the people that stick around have to fix and deal with all of it."

Ever since Claude Opus 5.5 released back in September, it feels like the modding scene has been going through a rollercoaster, and it's impossible to know where exactly it's going to land. Whether the world of Nexus Mods and publicly available GitHub forks is going to start to die down like Mgamerz thinks it will is anyone's guess. But one thing's for sure: Once The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel drops, modding is going to be a completely different animal than the Skyrim days, if Bethesda's next game is even moddable at all.

items.title: BioWare 可能已经死了，但 Mod 制作者已将《质量效应 3》的多人游戏重建为传奇版
items.summary: When the Mass Effect Legendary Edition came out in 2021, it included the single player campaign of all three o

content.v: https://assets-prd.ignimgs.com/2026/11/06/masseffect-multiplayermod-interview-blogroll-1793999260678.jpg

When the Mass Effect Legendary Edition came out in 2021, it included the single player campaign of all three original games, along with all the DLC. But while all the story content you could ever want was included, Mass Effect 3's multiplayer mode was conspicuously absent, despite having a dedicated fanbase.

Now, just a few weeks after EA's shutdown of BioWare , a team of modders has successfully ported Mass Effect 3 's multiplayer to the Legendary Edition, with all the graphics and engine improvements that came with that re-release. The mod will be coming out on N7 Day – November 7th – and will be free to play, as long as you already own Mass Effect Legendary Edition.

I also got a chance to sit down with Mgamerz, who runs the ME3Tweaks team that created the mod, to talk about Mass Effect 3, and about the state of modding in 2026. And if you want to download the mod yourself, it's available now on Nexus Mods.
IGN: So, tell me a little bit about the project, and how you got started on basically porting the Mass Effect 3 multiplayer over to the Legendary Edition.

Mgamerz: Yeah, so my dev team, ME3Tweaks, and I run it. We ported Pinnacle Station back in 2021. Crazy effort. I don't know how we got that done in a two-month timeframe. And then we were doing other projects for two years, and then near the end of me working on LE2 Randomizer, which is a randomizer for legendary Mass Effect 2, someone discovered a copy of the Citadel in Mass Effect 2.

There's an area from the wards. I can't remember which game it was, but they found an area of the game that nobody knew about before, and you could load into and you're like, 'Well, this was clearly supposed to be something, and then they just never finished it.' It was a very early prototype. And it was like, 'Man, what if we could port something like that into another level?' And so I made this project called Project Wardle, Ward being the first part of it. (We have a bunch of stupid internal code names.)

And I eventually made it so we could port a Mass Effect 2 level into Mass Effect 3, and we fixed up the cover, because cover is just an unbelievable nightmare. It's very important for enemies to be able to use it. Gameplay's a huge component of why Mass Effect 3 is fun. And we got that working and then I was like, 'Well, man, what if we could port the multiplayer levels?' Because we did it for Pinnacle Station. We ported the old game. But Pinnacle Station is mostly just reused assets from Mass Effect 1.

Like 90% of it was just existing assets that they just reused. But multiplayer was totally different. It's like, yeah, none of this content exists. So the scope of work is just huge. So at the end of 2023, right as we finished LE2 Randomizer, literally on N7 day, I spun up a new Discord.

I invited a couple people and they're like, 'What's this Discord about?' I'm like, 'We're going to do something stupid. We're going to port [Mass Effect 3] Multiplayer.' And those were the first two messages I ever sent. I have some screenshots of it.

And then people were like, 'Yeah, you're joking, right?' And I'm like, 'No.' And then the last three years we've been working on it. It hasn't been constant. Last year I broke my arm, which set us back six to eight months.

But for the first two years, it was tons of prototyping. Within the first month of this project, we actually had multiplayer working. It was a proof of concept. And then we spent the next two years getting audio to port, from a different version of the audio engine because they upgraded it. It's like we got shaders building, which was a total nightmare because BioWare compiled the game with a bunch of sources that don't ship with the game.

And so we had to figure out 'how do we replicate that?' So that took a long time. And then it's like textures. We have a bunch more people that know how to do texture upscaling. The first two years is almost all prototype and then asset generation. We want to make it look good. We're planning stuff out, that kind of stuff. So that's really not how it started.
IGN: So, you basically built from scratch again? Did you take assets from the original Mass Effect 3?

Mgamerz: Oh yeah, the whole thing ports from it. It's not a one-to-one port. We're not just taking Mass Effect 3 multiplayer and dumping it into Legendary Edition and then, 'Hey guys, check out it's multiplayer, [as] you remember it.' Where we took a lot of extra steps, the lighting actually gets re-baked in Unreal Engine 4's light solver.

Essentially what that means is, imagine you have a light bulb in a room and if you wanted to project what the lights would look like, a light beam's going to hit your microphone and it's going to cast a shadow.

And then that light bounces off for you, goes into your closet and it bounces off and illuminates the closet a little bit from the inside. Unreal Engine 3 had a solver and that's how all of the lighting for all the Unreal Engine 3 games worked. But in Unreal Engine 4, they added like, 'Oh, we can do additional light bounces or we found a better statistical way to do light bounces.' And so you get crisper shadow edges or the more soft, like a grate covering on some maps. The light bounces through the grate, and unless you have super high resolution textures, it looks terrible. Mass Effect 3 is full of terrible light maps. If you look at them, you're like, 'Wow, it's just a big stair step of shadows and it looks bad.' And so we spent a lot of time upgrading that kind of stuff.

I modded Mass Effect 3 multiplayer for eight years before Legendary Edition came out, and there's a bunch of stuff I was like, 'Wow, I didn't even realize three of the character classes don't even use the highest-quality mesh.' So it's like BioWare made the Geth Infiltrator, and they made it at a high quality where it has all the polygons and triangles. And then as you get further away from the camera, it gets less triangles, because you can't see as much detail. But BioWare was just like, 'We're just not going to use the highest quality one. We'll ship it in the game, but you'll never see it.' And so it's like, 'Oh, well, we can just turn those on and it's an immediate quality upgrade.'

IGN: Was quality a big reason why you took on this massive undertaking to bring ME3 multiplayer to Legendary Edition? Because if I understand correctly, the servers for the original ME3 multiplayer are still working, for now at least.
Mgamerz: By the time we publish this, I don't know, man. N7HQ's gone, so I wouldn't be surprised if it disappears before.

Actually, the whole reason this project started, I was getting to the end of LE2 Randomizer and I was like, 'Man, I love Mass Effect 3 multiplayer.' I modded tons of stuff into it, and it was really fun.

I went back and I was like, 'I want to make a new one. I want to make a new mod.' I went back to it and I was like, 'These tools,' and I'm totally throwing myself under the bus, 'These tools suck. There's no debug tools. Everything is so immature compared to what we have in Legendary Edition, thanks to what BioWare changed for us.' And so I was like, 'Man, I'd rather just port multiplayer than have to deal with this awful development environment.'

items.title: 你在 RPG 游戏中做过的最艰难的选择是什么？

content.v: https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/ckZUwfxbakq5yXMJMfSmBW-1920-80.png

Welcome to Dungeon Master , PC Gamer's regular RPG column, where Online Editor Fraser Brown delves into PC gaming's most beloved and enduring genre. Grab a seat in our badly-lit tavern and please ignore the goblin puke.

We love a big RPG dilemma, don't we? Right up until the point where we actually have to make the choice and we stare at our screens for an uncomfortably long time, hoping we'll figure out a way to make a call and not feel absolutely terrible about it later.

For my money, the best—agonising, guilt-inducing—choices are the really personal ones. I love that Mass Effect lets me determine the fate of the galaxy in all these different ways, but it never gives me a reason to care about the rachni, for instance, or the council, so when I have to decide to save them or let them die, it becomes more of an abstract moral choice.

Disco Elysium , then, left me in tatters. It's more personal and intimate than a productive therapy session. There's a card you can read pretty early on, stuck inside a ledger, that opens the wound that Harry worked very hard—by abusing alcohol and drugs—to forget. If you toss it, you never get it back. That was a hard one. Is ignoring it a kind of liberation? Or are you just helping Harry hide from his trauma?

It's effective because it's powerfully relatable. You don't even need to have experienced a cataclysmic breakup to understand Harry in that moment. We've all got shit we'd really love to forget. Self-destructive choices that we made in a heated moment, leaving regret to constantly claw at us.

Relationship drama should be excellent fodder for RPG choices, but that rarely ends up being true. Usually they end up being friction free, but sometimes you'll be walloped with the classic trope of being forced to decide if they live or die—a cheap trick to force us to care about someone, even if they actually suck. Yeah, I'm talking about you, Ash.

That's why Geralt's romantic misadventures are so effective at spitting out challenging conundrums. The best thing about The Witcher 3 's approach is that you can choose not to make a decision. It's so rare for games to recognise that indecision is another choice.

I desperately wanted Geralt to be happy. He deserved it. But I could not figure out the best way to go about giving him his happily ever after. The depths of his feelings for Yennefer nudge you towards making sure they have a life together, but god she's toxic. She regularly makes him feel like shit. Triss actually seems to make him happy, but is that just the safe pick?

So I never made the choice. I told both of them I loved them, and they left me tied to a bed while they went off to get drunk. My inability to make a choice was the worst choice. But it also ended up feeling poignant—Geralt so often gets in the way of his own happiness.
OK, what about you lot? What's the toughest choice I've had to make in an RPG? Let me know in the comments.
